questions.title: Section A - Multiple Choice, Terminology, Matching, Chromosomes, DNA and Blood Groups

subQuestions.questionText:
Which ONE of the following is a reproductive isolation mechanism?
A) Breeding at the same time of the year
B) Adaptation to the same pollinators
C) Prevention of fertilisation
D) Sharing the same habitat
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
Prevention of fertilisation is a pre-zygotic reproductive isolation mechanism that prevents gene flow between species.

options.A: Breeding at the same time of the year

subQuestions.questionText:
The scientists who won the Nobel Prize for the discovery of the structure of DNA were …
A) Watson and Franklin.
B) Wilkins and Franklin.
C) Crick and Wilkins.
D) Watson and Crick.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C or D (2 marks)
The 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery of the structure of DNA was awarded jointly to Watson, Crick AND Wilkins. Both options C (Crick and Wilkins) and D (Watson and Crick) are accepted as correct.

subQuestions.questionText:
In a dihybrid cross, an animal with long ears (E) and red fur (R) was crossed with an animal with short ears (e) and black fur (r). Which ONE of the following could represent the genotypes of the parents?
A) EERR x eerr
B) EeRr x EeRr
C) eeRR x eerr
D) Eerr x EERr
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
EERR shows long ears and red fur (homozygous dominant for both); eerr shows short ears and black fur (homozygous recessive for both). This matches the phenotypes described.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which ONE of the following reduces genetic variation in the offspring?
A) Mutations
B) Random mating
C) Cloning
D) Random fertilisation
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
Cloning produces genetically identical offspring (asexual reproduction), thereby reducing genetic variation. Mutations, random mating, and random fertilisation all increase variation.

subQuestions.questionText:
Meiosis is best explained as a process that produces … daughter cells.
A) two haploid
B) two diploid
C) four diploid
D) four haploid
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Meiosis produces four genetically distinct haploid daughter cells from one diploid parent cell.

subQuestions.questionText:
Colour-blindness is a disorder caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Which ONE of the following is the genotype of a colour-blind person?
A) X^D X^D
B) X^D Y
C) X^D X^d
D) X^d Y
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
X^d Y represents a colour-blind male — he has only one X chromosome carrying the recessive allele, so the trait is expressed. Females need two recessive alleles (X^d X^d) to be affected.

subQuestions.questionText:
The study of the inheritance of mutations in mitochondrial DNA is an example of …
A) fossil evidence.
B) genetic evidence.
C) modification by descent.
D) cultural evidence.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
Studying inheritance of mutations in mitochondrial DNA is genetic evidence used to support evolutionary relationships (e.g., the 'Out of Africa' hypothesis).

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: The bonds that hold the two strands of a DNA molecule together.
subQuestions.memoText: Hydrogen bond(s) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: A genetic cross involving one gene and its alleles.
subQuestions.memoText: Monohybrid cross (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: Undifferentiated cells that may form any other cell in the human body.
subQuestions.memoText: Stem cells (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: The structures in the cell that form the spindle fibres.
subQuestions.memoText: Centriole/Centrosome (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: The phase of meiosis when chromosomes are aligned at the equator of the cell.
subQuestions.memoText:
Metaphase I/II (1 mark)
[Either answer is accepted since chromosomes line up at the equator in both Metaphase I (homologous pairs) and Metaphase II (individual chromosomes).]

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: A genetic disorder where blood does not clot.
subQuestions.memoText: Haemophilia (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: The formation of new species.
subQuestions.memoText: Speciation (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: Evolution characterised by long periods of no change alternating with short periods of rapid change.
subQuestions.memoText: Punctuated equilibrium (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the correct biological term: The study of heredity and variation in organisms.
subQuestions.memoText: Genetics (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following description applies to A ONLY, B ONLY, BOTH A AND B, or NONE of the items in COLUMN II.
Description: Found in the nucleus.
A: DNA
B: RNA
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Both A and B (2 marks)
DNA is housed in the nucleus, and RNA (mRNA) is also produced in and found in the nucleus before being transported out for translation.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following description applies to A ONLY, B ONLY, BOTH A AND B, or NONE of the items in COLUMN II.
Description: Random arrangement of chromosomes.
A: Anaphase II
B: Metaphase I
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B only (2 marks)
Random arrangement (independent assortment) of homologous chromosomes occurs at the equator during Metaphase I. Anaphase II involves separation, not arrangement.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following description applies to A ONLY, B ONLY, BOTH A AND B, or NONE of the items in COLUMN II.
Description: Site of meiosis in humans.
A: Testis
B: Somatic cells
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A only (2 marks)
Meiosis occurs in the gonads (testes and ovaries) to produce gametes. Somatic (body) cells undergo mitosis, not meiosis.

subQuestions.questionText: The diagram in the question paper represents a pair of homologous chromosomes in a plant cell. The alleles for two characteristics, seed colour (G and g) and plant height (T and t), are indicated on the chromosomes. Give the term used to describe the position of an allele on a chromosome.
subQuestions.memoText: Locus (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify parts A and C (from the homologous chromosomes diagram in the question paper).
subQuestions.memoText:
A — chromatid (1 mark)
C — centromere (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the process during which parts A and B exchange genetic material.
subQuestions.memoText: Crossing over (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: During which phase of meiosis does the process named in QUESTION 1.4.3 take place?
subQuestions.memoText: Prophase I (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText:
State the following for this plant:
(a) Genotype
(b) The characteristic that is homozygous recessive
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Ggtt (2 marks)
Mark 1: Gg (heterozygous for seed colour)
Mark 2: tt (homozygous recessive for plant height)

(b) (Plant) height (1 mark)
[Both alleles for height are 't' (recessive), making this characteristic homozygous recessive.]

subQuestions.questionText:
The diagram in the question paper represents some nucleotides in a single strand of DNA. Give the LETTER of the part that represents a:
(a) Sugar molecule
(b) Phosphate molecule
(Refer to the DNA nucleotide diagram showing parts X and Y, with bases T, G, A, C.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Y (1 mark) — represents the sugar (deoxyribose), shown as the pentagon shape
(b) X (1 mark) — represents the phosphate, shown as the circle

subQuestions.questionText: How many nucleotides are represented in the diagram?
subQuestions.memoText:
4/Four (1 mark)
[Each nucleotide consists of a phosphate, a sugar and a nitrogenous base. There are four bases (T, G, A, C) shown.]

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the nitrogenous bases (from top to bottom as indicated by the arrow) of the complementary DNA strand of this molecule.
subQuestions.memoText:
A; C; T; G (must be in correct order) (1 mark)
[Original strand: T-G-A-C → complementary: A-C-T-G (using base-pairing rules: A-T, C-G)]

subQuestions.questionText: Name TWO processes that require the two strands of a DNA molecule to separate into single strands as shown in the diagram.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: (DNA) replication
Mark 2: Transcription/Protein synthesis
(Mark first TWO only)

subQuestions.questionText:
The table in the question paper shows the blood groups of the members of a family: Father A, Mother AB, Daughter A, Son 1 O, Son 2 B. Two children are biological offspring; one is adopted.
(a) How many different phenotypes for blood group appear in this family?
(b) How many possible genotypes are there for blood group AB?
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 4/Four (1 mark)
[Blood groups present: A, AB, O, B = four different phenotypes]

(b) 1/One (1 mark)
[Blood group AB only has one possible genotype: I^A I^B (co-dominance requires both alleles).]

subQuestions.questionText: Give the genotype of the father.
subQuestions.memoText:
I^A i (2 marks)
Mark 1: I^A (one A allele)
Mark 2: i (one recessive allele — needed because Son 1 has blood group O/genotype ii, meaning he must have inherited an i allele from each parent)

subQuestions.questionText:
Which member of the family:
(a) Has the genotype ii
(b) Has co-dominant alleles
(c) Is adopted
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Son 1 (1 mark) — blood group O is genotype ii (homozygous recessive)
(b) Mother (1 mark) — blood group AB shows co-dominance (both I^A and I^B are expressed)
(c) Son 1 (1 mark) — Son 1 cannot be biologically related because the mother is AB (genotype I^A I^B) and cannot pass on an i allele needed for blood group O

questions.title: Section B - Protein Synthesis, Karyotypes, Incomplete Dominance and Pedigree Analysis

subQuestions.questionText:
Haemoglobin is a protein found in blood that carries oxygen. The beta chain in normal haemoglobin has amino acid sequence: Val-His-Leu-Thr-Pro-Glu-Glu. In Haemoglobin S, position 6 is Val instead of Glu. The DNA base triplets coding for amino acids are given: CAC=Val, GTG=His, GAC=Leu, TGA=Thr, GGA=Pro, CTC=Glu.
Give the:
(a) DNA base triplet for amino acid 3 (Leu)
(b) mRNA codon for amino acid 4 (Thr)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) GAC (1 mark)
[Amino acid 3 is Leu, which is coded by the DNA base triplet GAC.]

(b) ACU (2 marks)
[Amino acid 4 is Thr. DNA triplet for Thr = TGA. The mRNA codon is complementary to the DNA template: T→A, G→C, A→U, giving ACU.]
Mark 1: Correct base pairing
Mark 2: U used instead of T (RNA-specific)

subQuestions.questionText: What is a change in the sequence of DNA base triplets called?
subQuestions.memoText: (Gene) mutation (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Use the information in the tables to explain how a change in the sequence of the DNA base triplets results in the formation of haemoglobin S, rather than normal haemoglobin.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: CTC on the DNA changed to CAC
Mark 2: Codons (on the mRNA) changed/GAG changed to GUG
Mark 3: Anticodons (on tRNA) changed/CUC replaced by CAC
Mark 4: which resulted in a different amino acid/Val

subQuestions.questionText: Describe how a person with haemoglobin S would be affected.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The cells will not receive enough oxygen
Mark 2: resulting in reduced cellular respiration/a person lacking energy/becoming tired/anaemia

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the process of translation during protein synthesis.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for each of the following points (max 6):
- Each tRNA carries an amino acid
- When the anticodon on the tRNA
- matches the codon on the mRNA
- the tRNA brings the (required) amino acid to the ribosome
- Amino acids become attached by peptide bonds
- to form the (required) protein

subQuestions.memoText:
The factors/alleles that control a characteristic separate (during meiosis) so that only one is present in each gamete (2 marks)
Mark 1: factors/alleles separate during meiosis
Mark 2: only one is present in each gamete

subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A person with Down syndrome will have 3 chromosomes
Mark 2: at position number 21

subQuestions.questionText: In rabbits, fur colour may be black, white or grey. The inheritance is controlled by two alleles: Black fur (B) and White fur (W). Explain why fur colour in rabbits is an example of inheritance with incomplete dominance.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The grey fur colour is an intermediate phenotype/a blend of black and white
Mark 2: This indicates that neither of the alleles is dominant

subQuestions.questionText: Use a genetic cross to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring when a grey male mates with a black female.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 COMPULSORY marks + Any 4 (Total 6 marks):

P1 Phenotype: Grey x Black
Genotype: BW x BB
[Meiosis label]
Gametes: B, W x B, B
[Fertilisation label]
F1 Genotype: BB, BB, BW, BW* (1 COMPULSORY mark)
F1 Phenotype: Black, Grey* (1 COMPULSORY mark for showing both Black AND Grey offspring)

P1 and F1 must show 'Meiosis' and 'Fertilisation' labels.

Alternative Punnett square layout:
   |  B  |  B
B  | BB  | BB
W  | BW  | BW
[1 mark for correct gametes; 1 mark for correct genotypes*]
F1 Phenotype: Black, Grey*

*2 compulsory marks + any 4 from: P1 phenotype, P1 genotype, gametes, meiosis label, fertilisation label, F1 genotype, F1 phenotype.

subQuestions.questionText: In humans, the ability to taste a certain substance is controlled by the dominant allele T. The pedigree diagram in the question paper shows the inheritance of this trait. What does the term 'dominant allele' mean?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for either:
- The dominant allele is always expressed (in the phenotype) when in the heterozygous condition
OR
- The dominant allele masks/hides the (phenotype of the) recessive allele

subQuestions.questionText:
Give the:
(a) LETTER of a female in the F1-generation who is a taster
(b) Genotype of individual J
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) N (1 mark)
[N is shown as a filled circle (female taster) in the F1 generation.]

(b) Tt (1 mark)
[J is heterozygous — see explanation in 2.5.3]

subQuestions.questionText: Use evidence from the diagram to support your answer to QUESTION 2.5.2(b).
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 4 marks for ONE of the following sets:

Option 1:
Mark 1: J is a taster and therefore must have one dominant allele/T
Mark 2: Individual K is tt (non-taster)
Mark 3: Individual O is a non-taster/is homozygous recessive/tt
Mark 4: She must have inherited a recessive allele/t from each parent — therefore J must have one recessive allele/t

OR

Option 2:
Mark 1: J is a taster and therefore must have one dominant allele/T
Mark 2: If J is homozygous dominant/TT
Mark 3: and K is homozygous recessive/tt
Mark 4: then it is not possible to have child (O) who is homozygous recessive/tt — as she must have inherited a recessive allele/t from each parent

questions.title: Section B - Human Evolution, Variation in Cows, Flightless Birds and Tawny Owls

subQuestions.questionText: There are anatomical differences between African apes and humans. There are also characteristics that they share. Name ONE characteristic of the hand that African apes share with humans.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for any ONE of the following (Mark first ONE only):
- Bare fingertips/nails instead of claws
- Opposable thumbs/gripping ability
- Fingerprints
- Five fingers

subQuestions.questionText: Tabulate THREE differences between the skulls of African apes and humans.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks: Table (1 mark) + Any 3 differences (3 x 2 = 6 marks). Mark first THREE only. (Total 7 marks)

Table should compare African apes vs Humans with corresponding rows. Possible differences:

African apes | Humans
- Small cranium | Large cranium
- Brow ridges well developed | Brow ridges not well developed
- Large canines | Small canines
- Palate is long and rectangular/U-shaped | Palate is small and semicircular/C-shaped
- Large jaws | Small jaws
- More protruding jaws/prognathous | Less protruding jaws/non-prognathous
- Cranial ridges present | No cranial ridge
- Foramen magnum in a backward position | Foramen magnum in a forward position
- Sloping face | Flat face
- Less developed zygomatic arch | More developed zygomatic arch
- Less developed chin | More developed chin
- Diastema between the teeth | No diastema between the teeth

[1 mark for tabulation + 2 marks for each correct comparison (one mark per side of table for the difference chosen)]

subQuestions.questionText: Give TWO characteristics of the pelvis of a bipedal organism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for any TWO of the following (Mark first TWO only):
- Short and
- wide/broad
- Cup-shaped

subQuestions.questionText: The fat content of cow's milk may vary between 2,6% and 5%. The data table provided shows the number of cows in each fat content range: 2,6–3,0 (11 cows), 3,1–3,5 (66 cows), 3,6–4,0 (93 cows), 4,1–4,5 (61 cows), 4,6–5,0 (15 cows). Draw a histogram to represent the results of the survey.
subQuestions.memoText:
Guideline for assessing the graph (6 marks):

Correct type of graph (T) — 1 mark: Histogram drawn (bars touching each other since data is continuous)

Caption of graph (C) — 1 mark: Both variables included (e.g., 'The number of cows producing milk with different fat content')

Axes labels (L) — 1 mark: X-axis (Fat content (%)) and Y-axis (Number of cows) correctly labelled with units

Scale for X- and Y-axis (S) — 1 mark: Same width of bars for X-axis AND correct scale for Y-axis

Plotting of bars (P) — up to 2 marks:
- 1 mark for 1 to 4 bars plotted correctly
- 2 marks for all 5 bars plotted correctly (11, 66, 93, 61, 15)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the percentage of the farmer's cows that produce low-fat milk (milk with a fat content of 3% or less). Show ALL your working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Working:
Total cows = 11 + 66 + 93 + 61 + 15 = 246
Cows producing low-fat milk (≤ 3%) = 11

$$\frac{11}{246} \times 100 = 4.47\%$$ (Accept 4,5%)

Mark 1: Correct numerator (11) over correct total (246)
Mark 2: Multiplication by 100
Mark 3: Final answer = 4,47% (or 4,5%)

subQuestions.questionText: State the type of variation that occurs in the cows, based on the evidence in the table.
subQuestions.memoText: Continuous variation (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give an explanation for your answer to QUESTION 3.2.3.
subQuestions.memoText: There is a range of intermediate phenotypes/the fat content % is a range (1 mark)

subQuestions.memoText:
Emu and Cassowary (2 marks - 1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Use information in the diagram to describe how biogeography supports the theory of evolution.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for any 4 of the following points (max 4 marks):
- A flightless common ancestor
- existed on one continent
- Due to continental drift the original population split
- and each population evolved independently

- Each continent now has a different species of flightless bird

subQuestions.questionText: Describe how it can be proven that ostriches and rheas are different species.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE of the following sets:

Option 1:
Mark 1: Allow time for them to interbreed/try to interbreed
Mark 2: If they produce infertile offspring/cannot interbreed, they are different species

OR

Option 2:
Mark 1: Conduct DNA analysis and
Mark 2: check for differences

subQuestions.questionText: There is variation in tawny owls. Some are white and others are brown. Scientists studied these owls over 30 years (1980–2010) to determine the effect of climate change on their survival, with increasing global temperatures and less snow each year. The graph in the question paper shows the number of tawny owls of each colour that survived every year. Identify the dependent variable in this investigation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Survival of the owls (1 mark)
[Also accept: Number of tawny owls of each colour that survived]

subQuestions.questionText: What conclusion can be made about the suitability of each colour owl to survive in more snow?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for either:
- The brown owls are less suited to survive than the white owls
OR
- The white owls are more suited to survive than the brown owls

[White owls are camouflaged in snow; brown owls are more visible to predators in snowy conditions.]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the results obtained from 2000 to 2010 for the white owls.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: There is a decrease in the number of white owls because
Mark 2: there is less snow and
Mark 3: white owls will not be camouflaged/will be more visible to predators

subQuestions.questionText: Describe how the scientists determined the number of owls that survived each year.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: They counted/sampled the number of owls at the beginning of the 4-month period
Mark 2: and again at the end
Mark 3: Then they calculated the difference between the two numbers

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE variable that was kept the same.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for any ONE of the following (Mark first ONE only):
- Time period/4 months
- Population
- Season/winter
- Method of calculation

questions.title: Section C - Essay: Evolution of Long Tails in Spider Monkeys

subQuestions.questionText:
Modern spider monkeys live high up in trees. They have very long tails which they use to hold on to branches. This reduces their risk of falling to the ground where they could be attacked by predators. The ancestor of spider monkeys had a much shorter tail.

Use Lamarck and Darwin's theories to explain why all spider monkeys have long tails and how artificial selection could have produced the same result.

Content: (17)
Synthesis: (3)

NOTE: NO marks will be awarded for answers in the form of a table, flow charts or diagrams.
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MEMO — Total: 20 marks (Content: 17 + Synthesis: 3)

LAMARCK (J) — Award marks for any 6 of the following (max 6):
- He would use his law of use and disuse
- and law of inheritance of acquired characteristics
- The ancestor of spider monkeys had short tails
- The ancestors continually stretched/used their tails
- to be able to hold on to tree branches
- As a result, their tails became longer
- and this characteristic was passed on to the next generation

DARWIN (D) — Award marks for any 8 of the following (max 8):
- Evolution occurs by natural selection
- There was variation in the ancestral population
- Some spider monkeys had short tails
- and some had long tails
- Those with short tails could not hold onto tree branches/fell on the ground
- They died/were attacked by predators
- The spider monkeys with long tails were able to hold on to tree branches/did not fall to the ground
- and survived/were not attacked by predators
- and reproduced
- The characteristic for long tails was passed to the offspring

ARTIFICIAL SELECTION (A) — Award marks for any 3 of the following (max 3):
- Humans select the spider monkeys with
- the long tails
- and mate them to produce offspring with long tails
- This is repeated over many generations

SYNTHESIS (3 marks) — Assessing the presentation of the essay:

• Relevance (R) — 1 mark: Only information relevant to describing the evolution of long tails in spider monkeys (in terms of Lamarck, Darwin, and Artificial selection) is included. There is no irrelevant information.

• Logical sequence (L) — 1 mark: The description of the evolution of long tails for each of Lamarck, Darwin, and Artificial selection is logical and sequential.

• Comprehensive (C) — 1 mark: At least the following minimum content is provided:
  - Lamarck (J: 4/6)
  - Darwin (D: 5/8)
  - Artificial selection (A: 2/3)

NOTE: NO marks awarded for answers in the form of a table, flow charts or diagrams.
